title: Tagliatelle ai funghi
subtitle: Egg pasta ribbons with mixed mushrooms, garlic, and parsley
excerpt: Tagliatelle ai funghi is a simple northern Italian pasta: broad egg-pasta ribbons dressed with a quick sauté of mushrooms, garlic, butter, and parsley. It comes together in 20 minutes and depends almost entirely on the quality of the mushrooms. A mix of chestnut and dried porcini gives the best depth.
sourceNotes: Northern Italian home-cooking tradition, particularly associated with Emilia-Romagna where fresh tagliatelle and woodland mushrooms are foundational. Methods drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992).

glossaryTerms.definition: Long, flat egg-pasta ribbons from Emilia-Romagna, about 8 mm wide; the original pasta for Bolognese sauce and a natural match for mushroom and butter sauces.

content.text: Tagliatelle ai funghi is one of the simplest Italian pasta dishes: broad

tossed with garlicky mushrooms, butter, and fresh parsley. The flavour depends on the mushrooms. A mix of fresh chestnut mushrooms and a small amount of soaked dried porcini gives depth without much extra work.

items.prepNote: soaked in 150 ml warm water for 20 minutes, then chopped; keep the liquid

content.text: Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil and half the butter in a wide frying pan over high heat. Add {{chestnut-mushrooms}} of sliced chestnut mushrooms in a single layer if possible. Cook without stirring for 3 minutes to get some colour. Toss and cook for 2 minutes more. Add the porcini and the soaking liquid (poured carefully, leaving the gritty sediment). Add {{garlic}} of sliced garlic and cook for 2 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a glossy coating. Season well.

Cook {{pasta-dried}} of tagliatelle in a large pot of salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a mug of pasta water, then drain. Toss the pasta into the mushroom pan with the remaining {{unsalted-butter}} of butter, adding pasta water to loosen. Add the parsley, toss once more, and serve with Parmesan.

items.symptom: Mushrooms are soggy rather than golden
items.cause: Pan was too crowded or heat too low, so they steamed.
items.fix: Cook in two batches, or increase the heat and resist stirring for the first 3 minutes.
The porcini and their soaking liquid add concentrated flavour that chestnut mushrooms alone cannot match. A splash of white wine added before the porcini liquid also helps.

content.text: Mushroom pasta belongs to the wooded hills of Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany, and Umbria, where porcini fill the autumn markets. Dried porcini have always been the home-cook's answer for months when fresh ones are not available. Soaked and added to chestnut mushrooms, they turn a simple pasta into something much better.
